sections.title: How does the Hyperfocal distance calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hyperfocal distance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports enlargement factor in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sensor size and the aperture f-stop); then you type in the print width, the print height, the visual acuity and the standard viewing distance.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hyperfocal distance calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Enlargement factor=print width ÷ Sensor width
Sensor height=print height ÷ enlargement factor
Sensor height=print height × Sensor width ÷ print width
Circle of confusion limit=(actual viewing distance ÷ (enlargement factor × standard viewing distance × visual acuity))
Lens focal length (f)=-1 ÷ 2 × focal ratio (N) × (actual viewing distance ÷ (enlargement factor × standard viewing distance × visual acuity)) + (1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (focal ratio (N) × (focal ratio (N) × (actual viewing distance ÷ (enlargement factor × standard viewing distance × visual acuity)) + 8000 × hyperfocal near limit) × (actual viewing distance ÷ (enlargement factor × standard viewing distance × visual acuity)))
Lens focal length (f)=-1 ÷ 2 × focal ratio (N) × (actual viewing distance ÷ (enlargement factor × standard viewing distance × visual acuity)) + (1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (focal ratio (N) × (focal ratio (N) × (actual viewing distance ÷ (enlargement factor × standard viewing distance × visual acuity)) + 4000 × hyperfocal distance) × (actual viewing distance ÷ (enlargement factor × standard viewing distance × visual acuity)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hyperfocal distance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the print width, the print height and the visual acuity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hyperfocal distance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns enlargement factor, derived from the print width, the print height and the visual acuity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hyperfocal distance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the print width, the print height, the visual acuity and the standard viewing distance, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter Sensor width in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Sensor width opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Sensor width = 0 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Hyperfocal distance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
